title: An MNAR shift moved an anchored transported contrast in a direction that differed from dataset to dataset, but the tipping set was almost always one interval
question: When an MNAR shift in imputed effect-modifier values enters a transported anchored contrast through several routes, is the contrast monotone in the shift, and is the tipping point a single value?
design: Two anchored individual-data trials with MNAR missing modifier values (equal or differing missingness), imputation plus a sensitivity shift over [-1.5, 1.5], STC standardized over a target law with a fixed or data-derived SD. 4 cells, 500 replicates each.
answer: Partly. The tipping set was a single interval in at least 96% of replicates (non-single 3.0% to 4.4%, under the registered 5%), so a single tipping point sufficed here. But the routes offset only on average: the mean slope of the anchored contrast against the MNAR shift was -0.004 to 0.030, while per dataset its SD was 0.10 to 0.14 and it was positive in 48% to 62% of datasets. The direction in which an MNAR departure moves the contrast was not predictable from the design, so sensitivity analyses must explore both directions.
findings: Registered branch: cancellation without non-unique tipping sets (flat curves in up to 6.4% of replicates with differing missingness).
Curves were non-monotone over the shift range in 77% to 80% of replicates but crossed the decision threshold in more than one interval in at most 4.4%.
The decision reversed somewhere in [-1.5, 1.5] in 29% to 30% of replicates.
not_answered: Two anchored individual-data trials rather than a disconnected component network; one imputation per shift; congenial imputation; one MNAR mechanism; tipping set defined by the point estimate's sign. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Marginal log odds ratio B versus A in the target, as a function of the MNAR shift
methods_compared: imputation plus shift with STC standardization, integration law fixed or from completed data
n_sim: 500 per cell, 4 cells, 31 shift values each
